PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 87 — Lesson 111: Acne, Rosacea & Hidradenitis Suppurativa

FNP-level goal: Distinguish common inflammatory facial and follicular disorders, choose a safe first management step, prevent scarring and medication harm, and recognize when the patient needs urgent evaluation or dermatology collaboration.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate acne vulgaris, papulopustular rosacea, and hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) by lesion morphology, distribution, time course, and associated findings.
  • Assess severity through pain, nodules, scarring, drainage, psychosocial burden, pregnancy potential, medications, and treatment response—not by lesion count alone.
  • Use antimicrobial stewardship in acne and understand why topical or oral antibiotic monotherapy is a poor long-term strategy.
  • Recognize patients who may need early dermatology care, isotretinoin evaluation, procedural care, ophthalmology assessment, or urgent infection evaluation.
  • Communicate without stigma: acne and HS are medical inflammatory disorders, not evidence of poor hygiene, contagion, or personal failure.

Part 1 — Start With the Morphology and Distribution

Many rashes are called acne in casual conversation. In primary care, the first task is to describe what is actually present: comedones, papules, pustules, deep nodules, diffuse erythema, telangiectasias, abscesses, tunnels, scale, or crust. Then ask where the disease occurs and how it behaves over time.

Acne vulgaris commonly produces open or closed comedones plus inflammatory papules, pustules, or nodules on the face, chest, and back. Comedones are a useful clue because they reflect follicular plugging.

Rosacea often presents with persistent central-facial erythema or flushing, papules and pustules, visible superficial vessels, and trigger-related flares. It generally does not produce the comedones typical of acne. Topical facial corticosteroids can worsen or mimic rosacea.

HS is a chronic inflammatory follicular disease with recurrent painful nodules, abscesses, drainage, tunnels, and scarring in intertriginous areas such as the axillae, groin, inframammary folds, buttocks, or perineum. A single simple abscess and recurrent HS are not the same clinical problem.

Part 2 — Acne: More Than a Cosmetic Complaint

Acne develops through a connected process: follicular plugging, altered sebum biology, proliferation of Cutibacterium acnes, and inflammation. The visible lesion is only one outcome. Deep inflammation may lead to persistent erythema, dyspigmentation, scars, and substantial anxiety or depression.

Ask about onset, menstrual or androgen-related pattern, acne-promoting medications or supplements, prior products, irritation, picking, family history, scarring, and the impact on school, work, relationships, and mood. Severe sudden acne with virilization or other endocrine clues requires a broader evaluation; routine testing is not necessary for every patient with acne.

Part 3 — Acne Treatment Principles

For many patients, topical therapy is the foundation. Benzoyl peroxide has antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity; topical retinoids normalize follicular keratinization and help prevent new comedones. A combination approach often addresses more than one part of the disease process.

Topical antibiotics should not be used alone because of resistance concerns. When an antibiotic is used, combining it with benzoyl peroxide and setting a reassessment date are important stewardship practices. Oral antibiotics may have a role in selected moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne, but they are not a maintenance plan without review. Response, adverse effects, adherence, and an exit strategy should be discussed at the start.

Deep nodules, active scarring, substantial distress, or inadequate response to appropriate therapy warrant timely dermatology involvement. Isotretinoin can be highly effective for severe, scarring, or treatment-refractory acne, but it requires specialist-directed safety monitoring and rigorous reproductive-risk counseling because of its major fetal risk. It is never a casual refill or an unsupervised workaround.

Part 4 — Reproductive and Medication Safety

Before prescribing acne medication, ask a respectful, private question about pregnancy possibility and contraceptive or pregnancy plans when clinically relevant. The safety of topical retinoids, oral tetracycline-class antibiotics, hormonal therapy, and isotretinoin differs; the medication choice must fit the patient rather than a generic algorithm.

Also ask about allergies, photosensitivity, renal or hepatic disease when relevant, drug interactions, and current skin products. A patient who stops every medicine because of irritation has not failed treatment—the plan may need gentler initiation, moisturizer support, simplified instructions, and a realistic follow-up interval.

Part 5 — Rosacea: Identify the Pattern and Protect the Eyes

Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory condition that may include flushing, fixed central facial erythema, papules, pustules, telangiectasias, burning, or sensitivity. Alcohol, heat, ultraviolet exposure, spicy foods, emotional stress, and certain skin-care products may be individual triggers, but patients should not be given a punitive or universal trigger list. A symptom diary can help identify their own pattern.

Management may include skin-barrier care, sun protection, trigger reduction, and phenotype-directed topical or systemic therapy. The FNP should also ask about gritty eyes, eyelid inflammation, eye redness, pain, photophobia, or vision change. Eye pain, photophobia, or reduced vision is not a routine skin follow-up issue; it needs prompt eye evaluation.

Part 6 — Hidradenitis Suppurativa: Recognize the Chronic Disease

HS is frequently delayed or mislabeled as repeated boils. Ask directly about recurrent lesions in the same folds, draining openings, malodor, scars, tunnels, pain, missed work, sexual-health impact, prior incision and drainage, and family history. Assess smoking, weight and metabolic health, mood, and symptoms that may suggest associated inflammatory disease without blaming the patient for any of these factors.

HS care is staged and multidisciplinary. Early disease may use anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial approaches, while extensive tunnels, scarring, refractory disease, or major quality-of-life impact often requires dermatology and sometimes surgical collaboration. Repeated isolated incision and drainage may relieve an acute fluctuant collection but does not treat the underlying chronic process or prevent recurrence.

Part 7 — Infection Safety in HS and Other Follicular Disease

Not every painful HS flare is an emergency, but a rapidly enlarging painful lesion, fever, systemic illness, spreading erythema, disproportionate pain, immunocompromise, or concern for a deep soft-tissue infection changes the disposition. Evaluate urgently when infection or sepsis is possible. Do not normalize severe pain or assume that drainage automatically makes the condition benign.

Part 8 — Differential Diagnosis Keeps Treatment Safe

Consider bacterial folliculitis, contact dermatitis, periorificial dermatitis, steroid-induced eruptions, fungal disease when morphology supports it, and medication-related eruptions. In a patient with facial pustules, the presence or absence of comedones, central facial erythema, eye symptoms, distribution, product exposures, and corticosteroid use can change the diagnosis and avoid months of ineffective therapy.

Likewise, an abscess-like lesion in the axilla may be an isolated infection, HS, an epidermal inclusion cyst, or another process. Recurrent location, multiple sites, scars, sinus tracts, and chronicity are high-value clues.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Scarring Acne

A 22-year-old patient has painful jawline nodules, new depressed scars, and worsening anxiety despite using an over-the-counter wash. The FNP documents lesion type and distribution, asks about pregnancy potential and medications, evaluates for acne-promoting exposures and safety concerns, begins an evidence-based plan that addresses more than one mechanism, and arranges close reassessment. Because active nodules and scars can cause permanent harm, timely dermatology referral for advanced options is appropriate rather than waiting through repeated ineffective short trials.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Do Not Miss Ocular Rosacea

A 49-year-old patient reports recurrent central facial burning and pustules plus gritty, red eyes. The absence of comedones and trigger-related flushing support rosacea. The FNP addresses skin care and treatment, but also asks about eye pain, photophobia, and vision change. Significant ocular symptoms require prompt ophthalmic evaluation; the safety decision is as important as the skin diagnosis.

Part 11 — FNP Case: Recurrent Axillary Draining Lesions

A 31-year-old patient reports painful axillary nodules every few weeks, drainage from old openings, and scars in the groin. This pattern supports HS rather than a one-time boil. The plan should address pain, infection red flags, comorbidities and modifiable supports, treatment stage, and dermatology referral. Shame-sensitive language matters: HS is not contagious and is not caused by poor hygiene.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Describe: lesion type, distribution, severity, chronicity, scars, tunnels, eyes, and systemic symptoms.
  2. Differentiate: acne with comedones; rosacea with central erythema/flushing and no typical comedones; HS with recurrent intertriginous nodules, drainage, tunnels, and scars.
  3. Screen for harm: scarring, pain, mental-health burden, pregnancy-related medication safety, ocular danger, and infection red flags.
  4. Treat deliberately: combine mechanisms, limit antibiotic exposure, support adherence, and reassess.
  5. Escalate: involve dermatology early for scarring/refractory acne or significant HS; arrange urgent or emergency assessment for eye danger signs or suspected serious infection.

Take-Home Summary

Acne, rosacea, and HS are common but clinically distinct inflammatory disorders. Accurate morphology prevents the wrong treatment. In acne, protect against scarring and use antibiotics responsibly. In rosacea, ask about ocular disease. In HS, recognize recurrence, tunnels, pain, and stigma as signs of a chronic disease requiring longitudinal care—not a sequence of unrelated boils. The FNP contribution is diagnosis, medication safety, symptom control, follow-up, escalation, and compassionate communication.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, current prescribing information, local protocols, specialist guidance, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
